quotes.text: Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark made highbrow synthpop their ethos. The likeminded duo of Andy McCluskey and Paul Humphreys was at its best when coupling its experimental, intellectual side – born from a shared love of Kraftwerk and urge to discover just how much the studio could shift the pop styles of the '80s – with, well, catchy music.

this album puts the creativity and ambition McCluskey and Humphreys were once proud of to one side. There is some mild experimentation that wishes only to meet quota, but mostly doddering pop arched by some of their most moaning vocals
prior OMD albums were at their best when focussing on melody, with a pinch of the abstract sitting idly by
Talking Loud and Clear is one of those interpersonal Kraftwerk clones OMD tend to do quite well; pretty synth loop, a bit of peace to round the album off.
Bauhaus Staircase is a fine contribution, it is the closest that any of the comeback albums come to leaching off of past successes without really trying anything defiant.

Rather than hire studio time to record the album, OMD co-founders Andy McCluskey and Paul Humphreys used their advance payment from Dindisc to build their own Liverpool recording studio, The Gramophone Suite.
McCluskey and Humphreys used cheaply-acquired instruments, as well as the low-end Korg M500 Micro-Preset (which had been paid for in many instalments).
Much of the content centres around war themes; McCluskey noted that the band were exploring "the lengths to which people would go in a situation beyond the norm".
Still generally a duo performing alongside a TEAC 4-track tape recorder christened "Winston", OMD enlisted Martin Cooper and Malcolm Holmes.
Kraftwerk, Neu! and Brian Eno served as key musical influences on the album, which showcased OMD's minimal synth-pop style.
Biographer Johnny Waller described the finished record as "basically a studio version of their live set".

The group were dissatisfied with the production values of Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark, Humphreys stating, "We didn't know what the heck we were doing half the time." McCluskey, however, feels that "in hindsight it now has a naivety and charm, and is full of energy".

Sounds' Des Moines proclaimed OMD to be "the most inventive of all the new Mersey[side] bands", while noting that they had "pulled off what is traditionally the biggest gamble in rock: playing totally engaging, satisfying music without the facility of the lead guitar".
This is the band's goth album, sort of: a moody, atmospheric record that found them eschewing melody in favor of melancholy.
Co-produced by Mike Howlett (ex-Gong), the album is in some ways a refinement of their approach as Andy McCluskey, Paul Humphreys and Malcolm Holmes focus on sounds, textures and patterns.

The sum effect does feel underdone, but I don't know if that's because the band didn't have the time to develop their songs or simply short-circuited the development process in favor of creating a specific mood/feel. It is a moody album, and that's clearly by design.

There's a wistfulness in this music that seems to take its cue from "Enola Gay," as though McCluskey and Humphreys were living in a world they couldn't change, and so accepted it with a resigned sadness.
It's an intriguing record, as electronic music was still a novel concept, and OMD was clearly pushing the fringes of the medium's frontier on these early albums.

I believe that Humphreys and McCluskey were trying to make a serious album – both thematically and musically, within their chosen medium of electropop. They succeeded, I also believe, in large part because of the novelty of synthesizers.
Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark corrected course, sort of, sailing for smoother waters on Junk Culture.
The rough edges have been polished smooth, except perhaps for White Trash and Junk Culture.
The band's experiments are contained to pop-funk (Locomotion, Apollo) and Afropop (All Wrapped Up), their moody excursions made lighter (Never Turn Away, Love and Violence, Hard Day).
The first two albums were icy cold, the third autumn crisp, the fourth a stormy affair, and here the gray clouds give way to sunlight.
What began as an English Kraftwerk was now beginning to sound like a John Hughes film.
The ghost of the old OMD is still in the machines, surfaced in strange sounds and exotic electronics.
Yet as new wave became the norm, the old revolutionaries traded in their pitchforks for fountain pens.
